title: Ikhfa (Hiding)
explanation: When noon saakinah (نْ) or tanween is followed by one of fifteen letters, the noon sound is hidden — pronounced with a light nasal sound (ghunnah) between a clear noon and full merging, held for about two counts.
detail: The fifteen letters of Ikhfa are: ت ث ج د ذ ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ف ق ك. The tongue does not touch the upper gum ridge as it would for a full noon; instead the sound resonates through the nose while the mouth is shaped for the coming letter.

title: Idgham (Merging)
explanation: When noon saakinah or tanween meets one of six letters (ي ر م ل و ن), the noon merges into the following letter. With ghunnah for ي ن م و, without ghunnah for ل ر.
detail: Idgham is not applied when noon sakinah and its following letter appear in the same word — in that case noon is pronounced clearly (izhar mutlaq), as in دُنْيَا, قِنْوَانٌ, صِنْوَانٌ, بُنْيَانٌ.

title: Iqlab (Conversion)
explanation: When noon saakinah or tanween is followed by the letter baa (ب), the noon sound is converted into a concealed meem sound accompanied by ghunnah.
detail: In the mushaf this is often marked with a small م above the noon. The lips close softly but do not fully press, producing a nasal meem held for two counts.

title: Izhar (Clarity)
explanation: When noon saakinah or tanween is followed by one of the six throat letters (ء ه ع ح غ خ), the noon is pronounced clearly — no hiding, no merging, no ghunnah beyond its natural length.
detail: These are called the huroof al-halq (throat letters) because their articulation point is the throat. The noon stays crisp and distinct before them.

title: Ghunnah (Nasalization)
explanation: A nasal sound held for approximately two counts on any meem (مّ) or noon (نّ) with shaddah.
detail: The sound resonates through the nasal passage, not the mouth. You can feel the vibration by lightly touching the nose while reciting إِنَّ or ثُمَّ.

title: Qalqalah (Echoing)
explanation: A slight bouncing echo produced on the letters ق ط ب ج د when they carry a sukoon — whether originally or due to stopping.
detail: The letters are remembered by the phrase قُطْبُ جَدٍّ. Qalqalah sughra (minor) is in the middle of a word; qalqalah kubra (major) is when we stop on a qalqalah letter at the end of a word, and the echo is stronger.

title: Madd (Elongation)
explanation: Stretching a vowel sound across two counts (natural madd) or longer (derived madd) when one of the three madd letters (ا و ي) follows a matching vowel.
detail: Natural Madd (Madd Tabee'i) = 2 counts. Derived Madds include Madd Muttasil (4-5 counts, hamzah after madd letter in same word), Madd Munfasil (4-5 counts, hamzah in next word), and Madd Lazim (6 counts, obligatory due to shaddah or sukoon).

title: Meem Sakinah
explanation: Three rules govern meem saakinah (مْ): ikhfa shafawi before ب, idgham shafawi before م, and izhar shafawi before all other letters.
detail: Ikhfa Shafawi — when meem sakinah meets ب, the lips lightly close and ghunnah is held. Idgham Shafawi — when meem sakinah meets another meem, they merge with ghunnah. Izhar Shafawi — all other letters; the meem is pronounced crisply, especially taking care before و and ف (which share the lips).

title: Laam Shamsiyyah & Qamariyyah
explanation: The laam in the definite article ال is either silent and merged (shamsiyyah / 'solar') or pronounced clearly (qamariyyah / 'lunar'), depending on the following letter.
detail: 14 shamsi letters (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن) cause the laam to be silent and the next letter doubled: الشَّمْس. 14 qamari letters (ا ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م و ه ي) allow the laam to be pronounced: الْقَمَر.

title: Tafkheem & Tarqeeq (Heavy & Light)
explanation: Some letters are always heavy (tafkheem), some always light (tarqeeq), and some change based on vowels.
detail: Always heavy: خ ص ض ط ظ غ ق. Always light: all others except ر and ل (in the name of Allah). ر is heavy with fatha/damma, light with kasra. The laam in الله is heavy after fatha/damma, light after kasra.

title: Waqf (Rules of Stopping)
explanation: When stopping at the end of a word, the last letter is made saakin. Tanween becomes a single fatha, and taa marbuta becomes haa sakinah.
detail: Mushaf symbols guide stopping: مـ (must stop), لا (do not stop), ج (permissible), صلى (continuing is better), قلى (stopping is better). Stopping mid-ayah is allowed if the meaning is complete; stopping where meaning is incomplete should be avoided.
